solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Dance with man briefly three times (3-3-3)

indicators.note: a brief word is cut short, so CHAP loses its last letter
tells you to write the piece out three times over

annotation.surface: A dancer is told to partner a man, but only briefly, and three times over.
annotation.walkthrough: CHAP is the everyday British word for a man. The answer is simply its stub CHA written out three times.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Cuban ballroom dance whose name imitates its triple step.

entries.clue: This case sadly leading to reprimand (8)

indicators.note: something done sadly is done badly, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A regrettable case ends with someone being told off.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is the first two words together; 'sadly' reads like a comment on the case.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to scold someone severely for a fault.

entries.clue: Husband welcomed by breakdown service, I see (3)

indicators.note: the welcomed letter is taken in by the other piece

blocks.note: the AA, Britain's Automobile Association, which rescues broken-down cars

annotation.surface: A husband is glad to see the roadside rescue van arrive.
annotation.walkthrough: The AA is the Automobile Association, the British motoring club best known for its breakdown recovery vans.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of sudden understanding, said when the penny drops.

entries.clue: He’s keeping Bill in hell (5)

indicators.note: one piece keeps the other inside it

blocks.note: a bill is an advertisement, AD, placed inside HES

annotation.surface: Someone holding on to an unpaid bill is having a hellish time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name or an invoice; here it is a poster, an AD.
annotation.definitionFit: The underworld of Greek myth, whose name is used loosely as a euphemism for hell.

entries.clue: Payment that involves careful thought (13)

blocks.note: a sum given in return for a service, the legal sense

annotation.surface: A fee that ought to be weighed up carefully before it is paid.
annotation.walkthrough: The payment sense is chiefly legal or jokey: a contract needs consideration, and a fixer works 'for a consideration'.
annotation.definitionFit: The legal sense is something given in exchange for a promise; the everyday sense is deliberate reflection.

entries.clue: Harmful substance in medicine’s rarely shown up (7)

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the next words
in a down clue, 'up' means the letters read from bottom to top

annotation.surface: A dangerous ingredient seldom turns up in a medicine.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored: the hidden run crosses 'medicine’s' into 'rarely', then reads upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the classic poisoner's element, the harmful substance of Victorian murder stories.

entries.clue: Young producer finding love in southwest (3)

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: zero in tennis, placed inside SW

annotation.surface: A young film or music producer falls in love while in the southwest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Young producer' suggests a youthful film maker; read it as one that produces young, a breeding pig.
annotation.definitionFit: A female pig produces litters of piglets, so she is a producer of young.

entries.clue: Shelter sought from horribly scary aunt (9)

indicators.note: the letters are made a horrible mess of

annotation.surface: A nephew looks for somewhere to hide from a frightening aunt.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a complete little story; the fodder is just the two words at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a place of refuge, once a church where fugitives could not be seized.

entries.clue: Indecisive period for the audience (4)

indicators.note: what an audience gets is the sound, not the spelling

annotation.surface: A spell of dithering, perhaps from a theatre whose audience cannot decide.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Period' is the part that is heard; the spelling comes from the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Lacking firmness of will: a leader without resolve is called feeble or indecisive.

entries.clue: A row about boy — one whose every wish comes true? (7)

definitions.text: one whose every wish comes true?

indicators.note: A DIN goes round the next piece

blocks.note: placed inside A DIN, after the A

annotation.surface: A quarrel breaks out around a lucky boy who always gets what he wants.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Row' is the noisy kind, a DIN, not a line. The question mark flags the definition as a playful description rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful description: the hero of the Arabian Nights tale owns a lamp whose genie grants his wishes.

entries.clue: Social worker in South America who calls on you each year? (5)

definitions.text: who calls on you each year?
definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the person who visits yearly

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: ants live in colonies, so an ant is a social worker; placed inside SA

annotation.surface: A social worker in South America makes an annual home visit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' looks like a job title; it is an insect that lives in a colony. The definition is the rest of the clue, describing Santa's yearly call.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful description: Father Christmas visits every home once a year, on Christmas Eve.

entries.clue: Sat around eating old man’s food (5)

indicators.note: to turn around is to face the other way, so the word's letters run backwards
TAS takes the next piece inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round to TAS

annotation.surface: Someone sat about helping themselves to their father's dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s after 'old man' is 'is': the whole wordplay is food.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the small Spanish snacks served with drinks are a kind of food.

entries.clue: Badly portrayed, as shark is? (9)

indicators.note: the next word's letters are badly arranged

annotation.surface: A complaint that sharks get an unfair press as killers.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests sharks are misrepresented, yet the answer admits they really are hunters.
annotation.definitionFit: A shark hunts and eats other animals, so the adjective for a hunting animal describes it.

entries.clue: Some foreign items catch fire (6)

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, a run inside the words

blocks.note: the run starts after 'fore' and stops before the final 'ms'

annotation.surface: Certain imported goods are a fire risk.
annotation.walkthrough: The run straddles the space between the two words, which is what hides it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to begin burning, the intransitive sense of setting alight.

entries.clue: Fails to intervene: stalls extremely busy (6,2)

indicators.note: take only the extremes, the first and last letters

annotation.surface: A market trader does nothing while the stalls around are packed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stalls' looks like a verb, delaying; it is the plural noun, market stands.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to look on without acting, as a bystander does.

entries.clue: Drug dealer who loves life in the fast lane? (5,8)

definitions.text: who loves life in the fast lane?

blocks.note: amphetamine is nicknamed after quickness; a trader in it

blocks.clueFragment: who loves life in the fast lane?
blocks.note: the everyday sense: someone who loves going fast

annotation.surface: A drug dealer who lives recklessly.
annotation.walkthrough: The first sense is a joke reading, speed being amphetamine; the real phrase is informal British for someone who drives or runs very fast.
annotation.definitionFit: Taken literally it is a trader in amphetamine; as a real idiom it is someone who loves driving fast.

entries.clue: Mythical beast eats old soldier (7)

indicators.note: the eater takes the next piece inside it

annotation.surface: A dragon devours an elderly soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old soldier' looks like one phrase; 'old' is the O and 'soldier' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a mounted infantryman, the name surviving in some cavalry regiments.

entries.clue: Criticise an old lady’s hat (6)

annotation.surface: Someone mocks an elderly woman's headgear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is slang for mother, MA; the ’s is 'is', joining wordplay to 'hat'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the woven straw sunhat, made in Ecuador but named after the Central American country.

entries.clue: Artificial material children’s writer initially ignored (5)

indicators.note: the first letter is left out

blocks.note: what children write and draw with

annotation.surface: A synthetic fabric that a children's author first overlooked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Children’s writer' suggests an author such as Enid Blyton; it is the thing a child writes with.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a synthetic fibre made from cellulose, sold as imitation silk.

entries.clue: Mature Republican beginning to investigate US prison (5)

indicators.note: take the first letter of the next word

annotation.surface: An older Republican starts looking into an American jail.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mature' reads as an adjective describing the Republican; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: fruit or cheese comes to full development over time.

entries.clue: Small sweet potato (4)

annotation.surface: A small sweet potato.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a real vegetable, but 'sweet' is a noun here: in Britain 'sweet' and 'pud' both mean dessert.
annotation.definitionFit: A colloquial word for the vegetable, from the name of a digging spade.

entries.clue: Picture stolen, dumped in river (5)

indicators.note: the stolen goods are put inside the next piece

blocks.note: slang for stolen goods, placed inside PO

annotation.surface: A stolen painting is thrown into a river by thieves.
annotation.walkthrough: Stolen goods are 'hot'; the Po is the crossword's favourite river.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the short form of photograph, a picture taken with a camera.

entries.clue: The writer’s urge to dazzle? (7)

blocks.note: the writer is = I am = I'M

annotation.surface: An author's craving to show off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter speaking of themself, so 'the writer’s' becomes I'M.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to strike people with admiration by a brilliant display.

entries.clue: Old priest’s daughter leaving food shop (3)

indicators.note: the daughter's letter leaves the word

annotation.surface: A priest's daughter walks out of the delicatessen.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s is 'is', not a possessive: there is no daughter of the priest, only a D to remove.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Old Testament priest at Shiloh who raised the boy Samuel.

entries.clue: Diary regularly censored for 24 hours (3)

indicators.note: every other letter is cut out

blocks.note: D, A and Y from DiArY

annotation.surface: A diary has been cut about, covering one day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Censored' reads as a comment on the diary's contents; 'regularly' says the cuts fall at every second letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The time the earth takes to turn once on its axis, measured as 24 hours.

entries.clue: Nobody desperately intent on joining army in the end (9)

indicators.note: the letters are thrown about in desperation
take the final letter of army

blocks.note: the last letter of armY, joining the fodder

annotation.surface: No one is desperate enough to sign up for the army in the end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nobody' looks like the subject of the sentence; it is the definition, an insignificant person.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun sense: 'a nobody' is a person of no importance or influence.
